reason: The molecule is a substituted aziridine with an exocyclic chain bearing a hydroxyl group. Since the aziridine ring is fixed and strained, the conformational stability is dominated by intramolecular interactions, especially possible O–H···N hydrogen bonding with the tertiary amine. I analyzed the geometry of each conformer by estimating the O···N and H···N distances from the given coordinates. Conformers with O···N < 3.0 Å and H···N < 2.4 Å are likely to have a stabilizing (though bent) intramolecular hydrogen bond, with shorter H···N distances corresponding to stronger contacts. These were ranked first, ordered by decreasing H···N distance. Conformers with O···N > 3.5 Å lack any hydrogen bond and are placed last, as they miss this stabilizing interaction. Within the non-H-bonded set, no clear discrimination is possible without further analysis, so they are listed in arbitrary order. Steric clashes and eclipsing interactions were not quantified, but no severe close contacts were apparent from the coordinates. The ranking is therefore primarily based on hydrogen-bond feasibility and proximity, with the note that differences among the top group are subtle.

All conformers share the same heavy-atom connectivity: an ethylamine attached to an α-cyanoacetamide unit (CH3–CH2–NH–CH(CN)–C(=O)–NH2). The main stability differences come from intramolecular hydrogen bonding and, secondarily, from nonbonded methyl–carbonyl contacts. For each conformer I measured the shortest candidate H-bond: N3–H (amine) to carbonyl O8, N9–H (amide) to amine N3, and N9–H to nitrile N6. Conformers with a short, well-formed H-bond (≈2.1–2.2 Å) are most stable; those with only weak contacts to the nitrile N (≈2.7–3.0 Å) are least stable. Close C1–O8 contacts around 3.2–3.4 Å in some conformers (e.g., 5, 30, 28) were treated as mildly destabilizing. The ranking below orders the conformers by the estimated strength of their best intramolecular H-bond, with tie-breaking by secondary clashes and by the slightly stronger donor/acceptor combination where distances were equal.

All conformers lack a favorable intramolecular N-H...O hydrogen bond: the N-H...O angles are consistently near 90° rather than the optimal ~180°, so stability is governed primarily by steric clashes. I estimated the shortest nonbonded contacts between the methyl groups and the oxygens: C12 (methyl on the alpha carbon) to the carbonyl oxygen (O7) and to the ether oxygen (O5), and C1 (terminal ethyl methyl) to O7. Larger minimum distances imply less steric repulsion. Conformer 4 has the largest minimum contact (3.16 Å) and is therefore most stable. Conformers 13, 25, 27 follow with minimum 3.11 Å and a C1...O7 distance >4 Å. Conformers with C1...O7 short (~3.24 Å), such as 2 and 1, are slightly worse. The next group (20, 30, 22, 10, 9, 7, 14, 19, 8, 11, 23, 29, 24, 6, 15, 17) shows decreasing minimum distances and/or short C1...O7 contacts. Conformers with C12...O5 <3.0 Å (16, 3, 18, 5, 26, 12) are more strained, and the worst are 21 and 28 with a very close C12...O7 contact of 2.80 Å. The ranking reflects these steric penalties.

I examined the intramolecular hydrogen bond between the hydroxyl group (O2-H) and the ether oxygen (O1). For each conformer I computed the O1...H(O2) distance and the O1...O2 distance. Conformers with O1...H < 2.5 Å have a strong intramolecular H-bond and are the most stable. Among these, shorter O1...H and O1...O2 distances indicate a stronger interaction, so I ranked them accordingly: 5, 28, 4, 29, 8, 19, 22, 9, 7, 6, 15, 14, 3. Next, conformers with O1...H around 2.8-3.1 Å (20, 18, 25, 12, 13) have weaker or marginal H-bonding and are less stable. Then come conformers without effective H-bonding (O1...H >3.4 Å). Among those, I placed those with slightly shorter O1...O2 distances (2, 21, 16) before the rest (11, 10, 27, 1, 23, 24, 17, 26, 30), as they may have minor dipole alignment but no real H-bond. The differences within the non‑H‑bonded set are subtle, so the ordering there is approximate. The final ranking reflects this qualitative stability scale.

The molecule is a substituted cyclopropane diol (C7H14O2). The main stabilizing interaction is intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bonding between the two hydroxyl groups. I extracted the two O atoms and their attached H atoms from each conformer and computed O...O distances. Conformers with O...O < 3.0 Å are likely to form an H-bond; shorter distances generally imply stronger H-bonds if the H is oriented toward the acceptor. The shortest distances are found for conformers 28 (2.66 Å), 22 (2.70), 11 (2.72), 19 (2.73), 8 (2.74), 20 (2.76), 1 (2.80), 2 (2.83), 9 (2.87), 21 (2.87), 3 (2.88), 29 (2.89), 5 (2.91), 24 (2.92), 14 (2.96), and 26 (2.97). These are ranked highest. The remaining conformers have O...O > 3.5 Å, indicating no effective H-bond, and are placed lower. Among them, the order follows increasing O...O distance, with some adjustments for potential steric clashes (e.g., methyl groups near each other) and overall conformational strain. The ranking is approximate; uncertainties remain for conformers with similar O...O distances where the H-bond angle may vary, but the overall trend is clear.

The molecule is an N-substituted aziridine with a chiral carbon bearing ethyl and methoxymethyl groups. The relative stability is governed by steric clashes and torsional strain. I analyzed the coordinates for close nonbonded contacts, focusing on distances between the terminal methyl (C1), the ether oxygen (O), the methoxy methyl (C7), and the aziridine ring atoms. I computed approximate van der Waals overlaps using C...C (3.4 Å), C...O (3.22 Å), C...N (3.25 Å) sums. Key short contacts are between C1 and C6 (the CH2 adjacent to O), C1 and O, and C1 and N. Conformers with larger overlaps (sum of deficits) are less stable. The most stable conformers have no severe contacts and place the ethyl and methoxy groups away from each other and the ring. The least stable ones have short C1-C6, C1-O, or C1-N contacts, indicating eclipsing or gauche interactions forcing the bulky groups together. Some uncertainty remains due to the approximate nature of the analysis and the lack of explicit hydrogen positions, but the ranking reflects the relative steric strain inferred from the heavy-atom distances.

The molecule has two hydroxyl groups (on the carbon skeleton). In each conformer I located the two O atoms and the hydroxyl H atoms, then computed intramolecular O–H···O distances and O···O distances. A short H···O distance (<2.0 Å) with a reasonable O···O distance (~2.7–2.9 Å) indicates a strong stabilizing hydrogen bond. Conformers with such strong H-bonds are ranked highest, ordered primarily by decreasing H···O quality (shorter is better) and secondarily by O···O distance. Conformers with weak H-bonds (H···O 2.0–2.5 Å) are next. Conformers that lack any intramolecular H-bond are least stable; among those, extended (large O···O) conformers avoid steric crowding and are ranked above more folded ones that have close contacts but no H-bond. The ordering below follows these geometric criteria.

Analyzed the molecular geometry for intramolecular hydrogen bonding between the hydroxyl groups (OH on C9 and C5) and the carbonyl oxygen (O3). The most stabilizing feature is a strong O-H...O=C hydrogen bond. I computed O...O distances and checked the orientation of the O-H hydrogen relative to the acceptor. Conformers with O...O < 2.9 Å and H...O < 2.0 Å were classified as having a strong H-bond (1,3,5,6,11,13,15,21,26,28,29). The primary alcohol (O10) H-bonding to carbonyl gives slightly better geometry than the tertiary alcohol (O15) in many cases, so those occupy the top tier. Weak H-bonds (12,22,8,20,24) show O...O ~3.0 Å and H...O >2.3 Å. Conformer 7 has a close O3-O15 distance (2.77 Å) but the O-H points away, leading to likely dipole repulsion and thus is the least stable. Conformers without any favorable H-bond (2,4,9,10,14,16,17,18,19,23,25,27,30) are placed in the middle to lower ranks; their relative order is uncertain as steric and torsional effects are subtle.

The molecule contains one alcohol O-H donor and two carbonyl acceptors (aldehyde and ketone). I estimated intramolecular H-bonds by distances between the hydroxyl O/H and the carbonyl O atoms, and penalized close nonbonded contacts such as methyl-methyl (A vs F) and short O_ald...O_ket contacts. Conformers 20, 27, 8, 3, 29, 28, 18, 1, 19, 15, 13, and 26 have favorable OH...O=C intramolecular H-bonds; among these, 20, 27, 8, and 3 have the shortest O...O and H...O distances and better H-bond angles. Conformer 26 still has an H-bond but a close A...F methyl-methyl contact (~3.5 Å) makes it less stable than the other H-bonded forms. The non-H-bonded conformers were ranked mainly by how few repulsive close contacts they have: 9, 12, 25, and 11 appear relatively extended/unstrained, while 5, 10, and 21 have notable clashes/close carbonyl-oxygen contacts (e.g. O_ald...O_ket ~3.4–3.5 Å, methyl-methyl ~3.8 Å). Many of the middle non-H-bonded conformers are close in energy, so their relative order is uncertain.

The molecule is a 2-ethyl-5-(hydroxymethyl)-1H-pyrrole. The aromatic pyrrole ring is planar, so conformer energies are governed by side-chain rotamers and nonbonded contacts. I first identified the ring and substituent atoms from bond distances, then checked key intramolecular distances: the methyl carbon to the adjacent ring hydrogen (A-H18), the hydroxyl oxygen to the same ring hydrogen (O-H17), the N-H proton to the alcohol oxygen (HN-O), and the N-H proton to the methyl carbon (HN-A). No conformer has a well-aligned O-H...N or N-H...O hydrogen bond; the closest HN-O contacts in conformers 24 and 27 are ~2.4 Å with poor N-H...O angles, indicating steric repulsion rather than hydrogen bonding. Conformer 12 also has a severe HN to methyl hydrogen contact (~2.36 Å). Several conformers (2,3,4,9,18,21,28) place the ethyl methyl group close to the ring C-H (A-H18 ~2.86 Å), a clear steric clash. The remaining conformers avoid close repulsive contacts. Among the unstrained set, those with the hydroxyl oxygen at a favorable van der Waals distance from the N-H proton (~3.0 Å) are ranked higher because the contact is near the vdW minimum and electrostatically favorable; those with the oxygen farther away are still acceptable but slightly less stabilizing. Conformers with only mild methyl-ring contacts are placed in the middle. Differences within the middle and upper-middle groups are subtle, so their relative order is less certain than the separation of the badly clashing conformers at the bottom.

The molecule is a tertiary alcohol bearing a methyl, an aldehyde-containing ethyl arm, and a propargyl/alkyne arm. The dominant intramolecular stabilizing interaction is O–H···O=C hydrogen bonding between the hydroxyl proton and the aldehyde carbonyl oxygen, which can form a favorable six-membered hydrogen-bonded ring. Conformer 30 has the shortest and most linear such H-bond (H···O ≈ 1.94 Å, O–H···O ≈ 142°) and was placed first. Conformers 28, 17, 20, 23, and 10 also show strong O–H···O=C H-bonds with H···O distances around 2.07–2.14 Å; I ordered them by a combination of H-bond distance/linearity and absence of additional close contacts, giving 28 ≈ 17 > 20 > 23 > 10. The next set lacks a strong O–H···O=C H-bond but has modest C–H···O contacts or weak O–H···O approaches; 5 has the best aldehyde C–H···O interaction and no close alkyne contact, so it leads this tier. Conformers such as 13, 3, 16, and 8 have weaker compensatory interactions and, in some cases, close H···alkyne contacts that offset them. Extended conformers with no significant H-bond or severe clash, e.g. 24, 12, 4, 26, 14, 1, 18, 22, occupy the middle region. The least stable group consists of conformers with short nonbonded H(hydroxyl)···alkyne-carbon contacts near 2.4–2.5 Å and no compensating H-bond; among these, 19 has the shortest such contact and no favorable interaction, so it is ranked last. The middle- and lower-tier ordering is the most uncertain because the energy differences are subtle.

All structures are the same THF derivative (2-methyl-5-(2-hydroxyethyl)oxolane). The decisive stabilizing feature is an intramolecular O–H...O(ether) hydrogen bond between the side-chain OH (O15–H16) and ring O9. I computed H16...O9 distances: strong H-bond (~1.98–2.10 Å) in 3, 5, 12, 23, 17, 14; only weak/long in 27 (2.58 Å) and 2 (3.20 Å); all others >2.9 Å. Because the H-bonded conformers require a gauche orientation of the C10–C11–C13–O15 chain, they also carry one/two gauche interactions, but the H-bond overrides this and places them at the top. Among these, shorter H...O and more linear O–H...O angle put 3, 5, 12 slightly ahead of 23, then 17, then 14. The next best are the two conformers where the whole hydroxyethyl side chain is antiperiplanar (30 and 8), avoiding all 1,4 gauche interactions. 27 has a weak, poorly linear H-bond with a twofold gauche side chain, so it sits between the anti-extended forms and the single-gauche forms. The single-gauche no-H-bond conformers come next; those with the C–C–C–O unit anti (29, 15, 19, 9, 18, 7) are slightly better than those where the OH is gauche to the ring (1, 6, 11, 13, 10, 25, 16, 22), based on diminished steric contact between O15 and C1. The remaining doubly-gauche conformers without any H-bond (2, 28, 4, 21, 20, 26) are lower, and 24, with a skewed/eclipsed C–C–C–O arrangement, is the least stable. Uncertainties remain within tiers because ring-pucker differences are small and manual coordinate analysis cannot fully resolve them.

The molecule is an open-chain aldehyde/formimidate ester (CH3-CH(CHO)-CH2-O-CH=NH). The main stability factors are steric clashes between the imine nitrogen (N14) and the central/aldehyde carbons (C5/C6), because those atoms can come very close when the chain folds. Conformers 12, 20, 29, and 30 have extremely short N14...C6 distances (~2.1 Å) and N14...C5 distances (~2.6-2.8 Å), indicating severe nonbonded repulsion; these are ranked last. Conformers 18, 2, and 6 also have short N14...C6 contacts (~2.8-3.0 Å) and are therefore placed low. Many conformers with N14...C6 >4.5 Å and no sub-3.2 Å N...C contacts are more stable; among those, I favored conformers where the aldehyde oxygen is not brought close to the methyl group and where the N14...C5 distance is largest. The middle of the ranking is uncertain because the differences are subtle and no strong intramolecular hydrogen bond is apparent: the N-H proton points away from the aldehyde oxygen in all conformers, so the ranking is driven mainly by avoiding close heavy-atom contacts. The final order below reflects those geometric penalties, with the most stable extended, low-clash conformers first and the severely folded/clashing conformers last.

The molecule is a cyclohexene ring (one C=C between atoms 6 and 7) with a methyl group on the allylic carbon and a CH2OH group on the opposite saturated side of the ring. For each conformer I identified the half-chair ring conformation and examined: (1) whether the two substituents are far apart (C(methyl)···C(CH2OH) ≈ 4.8–5.1 Å, indicating a low-energy diequatorial-like arrangement) or close (≈3.4 Å, indicating a higher-energy diaxial-like/gauche arrangement); (2) short nonbonded H···H or C-H···O contacts involving the methyl and OH groups, which raise strain; (3) proximity of the OH hydrogen to the C=C as a possible weak O-H···π contact, but with poor O-H···π alignment in most cases, so I treated it as only a minor stabilizing factor. The most stable conformers are the extended, diequatorial-like structures with no strong methyl/OH clashes and the side chain pointing away from the ring. The least stable structures have close methyl···CH2OH contacts and/or severely short H···H or H···O contacts. Because many conformers differ by small torsional changes, the middle and lower portions of the ranking are uncertain, but the extremes are clear.

All conformers are the same flexible hydroxy-formamide. I used heavy-atom distances and, where possible, the hydroxyl/amide H positions to estimate intramolecular H-bonding. The most stabilizing interaction is O-H···O=C from the hydroxymethyl OH to the formamide carbonyl: conformers 7, 30, 21, 8, 9, 4, 23, and 14 have short O···O contacts near 2.8–3.0 Å and reasonably linear O-H···O geometries; 7 is clearly best because the H···O distance is shortest and the angle is good. The conformers 10, 6, 24, 25, and 15 have good N-H···O(hydroxyl) H-bonds, but this donor/acceptor combination is generally weaker than O-H···O=C, so I place them next. Conformers 1 and 5 still show O-H···O=C contacts but with longer/bent H···O arrangements. Conformers 19 and 18 have only weak N-H···OH contacts and are less stabilized. The remaining conformers lack a clear intramolecular H-bond; among them, 29 has an extended anti central chain and no severe contacts, while 3, 16, 13, 27, and 28 have gauche central torsions but no large clashes. The last group, including 2, 12, 26, 22, 20, 11, and 17, is folded and either poorly oriented or sterically crowded, especially 20, 11, and 17 with close methyl/polar contacts. The lower half of the ranking is the most uncertain, but the H-bonding top tier is robust.

The molecule is an aziridine-containing diol with two hydroxyl groups (O3 and O4) and one N-H. The dominant stabilizing factor is intramolecular hydrogen bonding. I estimated H···acceptor distances and O-H···A / N-H···A angles from the coordinates. Conformer 9 stands out because it forms a cooperative pair of good H-bonds: O4-H···O3 (H···O ≈ 2.08 Å, angle ≈ 134°) and O3-H···N (H···N ≈ 2.32 Å, angle ≈ 140°). Conformer 18 has a very strong, nearly linear O3-H···N H-bond (H···N ≈ 2.13 Å, angle ≈ 151°) but its N-H···O4 contact has a poor angle, so it is placed second. Conformer 21 has a strong O4-H···O3 H-bond plus a weak N-H···O3 contact and a relatively extended, unclashed backbone. The next tier contains conformers with one good O-H···O H-bond, ranked primarily by H-bond distance/angle and then by avoidance of a short 1,3 C1···O4 contact (syn vs anti arrangement). Conformer 13 has a short O-H···O and an anti C1···O4 arrangement; 12 is similar but has a closer C1···O4 contact; 6, 10, 1, 16, 20 follow among the remaining strong O-H···O set. Conformers 11, 7, 24, 14, 2, 30, 22, 29, 4, 27 have slightly longer or more distorted O-H···O H-bonds, with some suffering additional 1,3-syn strain. Conformer 15 has only a moderate/long O-H···O interaction. The remaining conformers lack a proper intramolecular H-bond; they are ordered by steric contacts and weak N-H···O proximity. Conformer 23 is the least sterically crowded of these; 5 and 26 have shorter but poorly oriented N-H···O contacts; 17, 19, 28, 25, 8 have similar or worse close contacts; 3 has the worst C1···O4 close contact and no compensating strong H-bond, so it is placed last. Differences within the middle and lower tiers are subtle, and the ordering there is uncertain.

The molecule is an O-alkyl imidate with a terminal hydroxyl: CH3-C(=NH)-O-(CH2)4-OH. The main intramolecular stabilizing effects are hydrogen bonds involving the imidate N-H, the ether oxygen, and the terminal O-H. I computed key H···A distances and X-H···A angles for each conformer. Strong, short, well-linear O-H···O(ether) hydrogen bonds are present in conformers 3, 18, 20, and 2 (H···O ≈ 1.87–2.02 Å, angle ≈ 153–159°); these should be the most stable. Conformers 12 and 13 have slightly longer/less linear O-H···O(ether) H-bonds, placing them next. Conformer 21 has a longer O-H···N(imine) H-bond with a good angle, and conformer 14 has two weaker/bent H-bonds (N-H···O and O-H···N); both should still be stabilized. Conformers 27, 19, and 30 have weaker N-H···O(hydroxyl) H-bonds, with 27 and 19 being better than 30 due to shorter H···O distances. All remaining conformers lack conventional intramolecular H-bonds and are ranked lower. Among these no-H-bond conformers, extended chains with minimal gauche strain are preferred over more folded ones; 23 is the most extended, while 1, 5, and 6 are the most folded and thus likely the least stable. The ordering of the middle no-H-bond conformers is uncertain because the energy differences are subtle and no thermochemical data are supplied.

The molecule is an open chain: N≡C-CH2-O-CH2-CH2-cyclopropyl. No strong H-bond donors are present, so stability is dominated by torsional strain (anti vs gauche/eclipsed), 1,4/1,5 steric contacts, and nitrile/ether dipole placement. I estimated the three main rotatable torsions C2-C3-O-C5, C3-O-C5-C6, and O-C5-C6-C7 from 1,4 distances (anti ~3.6-3.8 Å, gauche ~2.9-3.1 Å, eclipsed/skew ~3.2-3.5 Å). Conformers 27 and 2 are fully anti and extended, with no close nonbonded clashes, ranking highest. Conformers 23, 17, 30, 29, 12, and 9 have two anti torsions and one ideal gauche; they are very close in energy, with 23 having a possible O···H-C weak contact, while 17/30 have only the terminal nitrile-carbon gauche. The one-anti group (6,15,5,16,19,26,28,4,10,24,25) follows; those with two ideal gauche and one anti are better, and those with a skew 1,4 distance (~3.1-3.3 Å) are worse. The all-gauche and distorted conformers (3,18,1,11,14,20,21,8,13,22,7) are lowest because they accumulate gauche/skew interactions. Within the low group, ideal all-gauche helices are ranked above conformers with skew eclipsing contacts; the exact order near the bottom is uncertain.

All conformers share the same connectivity: a seven-membered oxacyclic ring containing one C=C alkene and a CH2OH substituent on the alkene carbon. With no strong conventional O-H···Oether hydrogen bond in most cases, the ranking was based on three geometric strain proxies: (1) eclipsing/gauche allylic interactions between the hydroxymethyl oxygen and the alkene CH carbon (short O···C(alkene) distances indicate the CH2OH is forced into an eclipsed, high-energy orientation); (2) transannular 1,4 and 1,5 contacts across the cycloheptene ring, especially C(ring)···O(ether), B···E and A···E contacts, where short values imply folded/eclipsed ring conformations and steric repulsion; (3) weak intramolecular O-H···Oether contacts, which can add small stabilization when the hydroxyl hydrogen actually points toward the ether oxygen. Conformer 23 stands out as the most stable because it combines a relatively extended, low-strain ring with the best O-H···Oether contact. Conformers 5, 24, 25, 28, and 29 are also extended with few severe transannular clashes and a hydroxymethyl group oriented away from the alkene. Conformer 7 has a weak O-H···Oether contact but suffers from close B···E/A···E transannular contacts. Several conformers (8, 13, 17, 3, 9) have moderately folded rings with a short C···O(ether) contact but otherwise avoid serious allylic OH···alkene eclipsing. Conformers 4 and 6 are also tightly folded but with less favorable side-chain placement. The severe group (18, 20, 2, 12, 14, 22) has very short C···O(ether) contacts plus close B···E and A···E interactions, indicating substantial ring strain. The least stable set consists of conformers with the hydroxymethyl oxygen very close to the alkene CH carbon (1, 10, 11, 15, 16, 19, 21, 26, 27, 30), especially where that OH···alkene clash is compounded by an already strained ring. Within this set, those with a balanced ring but only the allylic clash (27, 30) are slightly less bad than those with both allylic clash and severe folding (10, 26). Some near-degenerate conformers may differ by less than the uncertainty of this qualitative analysis, so the lower-mid ranking is approximate.

Each structure is the same tetrahydropyran-like ether with a terminal -CH2-CH2-OH side chain. The dominant stabilizing feature is an intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bond between the side-chain OH and the ring ether oxygen. Only conformers 30 and 15 place the hydroxyl hydrogen close to the ether oxygen: 30 has H...O ≈ 2.00 Å and an O-H...O angle near 164°, while 15 has H...O ≈ 2.05 Å and an angle near 153°. Therefore 30 is the most stable, followed by 15. For the remaining conformers, the side chain is either extended anti, which avoids close O...C contacts, or folded gauche with the OH oxygen approaching ring carbons at short distances (often O1...C5 ≈ 3.0–3.2 Å), producing repulsive van der Waals contacts. Extended anti conformers are ranked next, ordered mainly by slightly longer O1...C5 distances and absence of close contacts. Folded non-hydrogen-bonded conformers are ranked lower, with the worst being those showing the shortest O1...ring-carbon contacts (≈2.9–3.0 Å), especially 19, 1, 23, 7, 9, 11, and 27. The middle of the non-H-bonded list is uncertain because the energy differences are subtle and depend on small steric and torsional preferences.

The molecule is a substituted cyclobutane with two hydroxyl groups: a terminal CH2OH side chain and an OH on the cyclobutane ring. The dominant stabilizing feature is intramolecular O-H···O hydrogen bonding when the two OH groups approach each other. Four conformers show clear O···O distances near 2.9 Å with a donor H directed at the acceptor oxygen: 19 (side-chain OH donates to ring OH, O···O 2.88 Å, H···O 1.92 Å, and the ring is strongly puckered), 25 (same donor-acceptor pattern, O···O 2.87 Å, H···O 1.91 Å, but the cyclobutane is nearly planar), 30 (ring OH donates to side-chain OH, O···O 2.89 Å, H···O 1.94 Å, nearly planar ring), and 11 (ring OH donates to side-chain OH, O···O 2.92 Å, H···O 1.99 Å, nearly planar ring). The extra ring puckering in 19 relieves cyclobutane eclipsing strain, making it the most stable. Among the remaining three H-bonded conformers, 25 has the shortest H···O contact, then 30, then 11, but all have strained near-planar cyclobutane rings. Several non-H-bonded conformers (15, 23, 5) have O···O distances of 3.8–4.3 Å but the hydroxyl hydrogens point away, so the contacts are not stabilizing hydrogen bonds. The remaining structures have O···O distances >5 Å and therefore no intramolecular H-bond; their ranking is controlled by ring puckering and avoidance of severe eclipsing/steric interactions. Conformers with nearly planar four-membered rings and/or close nonbonded side-chain/ring contacts are placed lower. The ranking is approximate because subtle differences among non-H-bonded conformers are hard to separate without electronic-structure energies.

The molecule is an aldehyde with a central alkyne and a terminal aziridine. No strong N-H...O hydrogen bond is present; the shortest N...O contacts are still >4.5 Å, so the ranking is determined mainly by torsional strain and nonbonded contacts. I used two geometric diagnostics: the C2...C7 distance, which reports whether the C2-C3-C6-C7 chain is anti (~3.8 Å) or gauche (~3.0 Å), and the O...C6 distance, which reports whether the O=C-C-C arrangement is eclipsed/close (~2.8 Å) or more open/staggered (~3.5 Å). Conformers that are anti about the central C3-C6 bond and do not have O eclipsing C6 are the most stable. Those with one gauche C3-C6 interaction are intermediate. Those with an eclipsed O=C-C-C contact, even if C3-C6 is anti, are placed lower because of O...C/O...H crowding. Conformers combining the eclipsed O...C6 contact with a gauche C3-C6 arrangement are least stable. Within the groups, the ordering of very similar conformers is uncertain, especially among the many intermediate gauche conformers.

The molecule is a substituted tetrahydrofuran with a hydroxymethyl group at one ring carbon and a 2-oxoethyl (aldehyde) side chain at the adjacent ring carbon, plus a ring ether oxygen. The dominant intramolecular stabilizing feature is O-H...O hydrogen bonding between the hydroxyl H and the aldehyde carbonyl O. I estimated donor-acceptor distances and O-H...O angles from the coordinates. Conformer 26 has the shortest and most linear hydroxyl-to-carbonyl H-bond (H...O ~1.92 Å, good angle) with no severe close contacts, so it is ranked most stable. Conformer 2 and conformer 7 also have short, well-oriented H-bonds, but 2 is slightly better because 7 has a close H...H contact involving the hydroxyl H and a side-chain hydrogen. Conformer 21 has a longer but still reasonably linear H-bond, placing it fourth. After these, the differences are small. Conformer 15 shows a weak, bent O-H...O ether contact while being otherwise unclashed, so it is placed next. The extended, non-hydrogen-bonded conformers with no obvious O...O repulsion or very short intramolecular contacts (25, 12, 30, 23, 13, 8, 14) are grouped in the middle. Conformers with close O...O contacts but poor H-bond geometry, or with short carbonyl-H contacts, are ranked lower. The least stable are conformers where the hydroxyl oxygen and carbonyl oxygen are close without an effective hydrogen bond, especially 27, 4, and 22, because these arrangements create repulsive O...O interactions without compensating directional O-H...O bonding. Given the absence of thermodynamic data, the ordering beyond the top four is somewhat uncertain, but the rankings reflect steric clashes, hydrogen-bond donor/acceptor proximity, and oxygen-oxygen repulsion inferred from the coordinates.
